### Controlling for long-term trends and seasonality

In the sensitivity analysis, we varied the *df* of time splines from 1 to 10 *df* per year and evaluated model fit via AIC scores, as illustrated in Figure 1.

![](C:/Users/offne/OneDrive%20-%20University%20of%20Cambridge/III.%20Research/Chapter%202%20-%20Causal%20Inference/IV.%20Figures/SM_aic_1_season.png){#SM_aic_1_season width="100%"}

We can see the model fit gradually decreases until the *df* reaches 9 per year, and then remains stable. This output agrees with prior knowledge, and our final model will therefore use a time spline *df* of 9.

### Controlling for autocorrelations related to disease transmission

Figure X depicts an autocorrelation plot of the overall time series of hospital admissions in Himachal Pradesh. These plots indicate that strong autocorrelations are still present at lags 1 and 2 and other longer lags, which need to be evaluated.

\[FIGURE - ACF/PACF\]

We evaluated the value of including autoregressive terms of lags 0 to 7 in our model. \[REPORT\].

\[FIGURE - AIC line chart\]

In accordance with our results, our final model will include an autoregressive term with a lag of 1 to adjust for this residual autocorrelation.

### Choices of the flexibility of the lags of the exposure-response relationships

We chose a minimum lag period of 0 and tested a max period between 7 and 21 days across all outcomes. Across predictors, all models assumed a non-linear relationship (natural cubic spline with *df*=3) and applied a unconstrained distributed lag model with a *df* of 4, which is widely applied across DLNM studies \cite{xiao_exposure-response_2017}.

\[FIGURE - AIC line chart\]

### Choices of the flexibility of the shape of the exposure-response relationships

Considering the evidence above, we tested linear and non-linear relationship for all predictors. Non-linear models were described by natural cubic splines with *df*'s varied from 3 to 8.

\[FIGURE - AIC line chart\]

### Choices of the statistical models

We assessed how each model effected the shape of the temperature and total hospital admission relationship (Figure X). The differences were negligible, so we opted for a simpler model.

\[FIGURE - Shape comparison\]
